Notes / working principles / references

Things I keep coming back to.

Short pieces on technical delivery and architecture. The summaries are here; each title opens into a standalone note with the reasoning behind it.

01 Operating notes02 Technical notes03 Noteworthy

Operating notes.

SEP 2026

A schedule is not a dependency map. →

Dates answer “when.” Dependencies answer “what has to be true first.” A date attached to unresolved identity, access, source data or ownership is not a plan; it is a guess with formatting.

SEP 2026

Go/no-go should be boring. →

The final launch conversation should confirm evidence, not discover whether the team is ready. Readiness should already be observable before the meeting starts.

SEP 2026

Write down the decision, not just the meeting. →

Meeting notes preserve conversation. A decision record preserves the choice, rationale, owner, assumptions and conditions that would justify reopening it.

SEP 2026

RAID is useful only when it changes behaviour. →

A risk register matters when a risk changes sequencing, scope, ownership, monitoring or a stakeholder decision. Otherwise it is administration.

Technical notes.

SEP 2026

200 OK is not the outcome. →

A successful request proves that one layer accepted something. It does not prove identity, profile data, eligibility, journey behaviour or customer outcome.

SEP 2026

SDK vs REST is usually an ownership question. →

Client behaviour should usually originate where the behaviour happens. Server-authoritative outcomes should originate where the business transaction becomes true.

SEP 2026

Events describe moments. Attributes describe state. →

“Customer booked Paris” and “customer has three lifetime bookings” are both useful, but they are different shapes of information and should not be modeled interchangeably.

SEP 2026

The system boundary is where I start debugging. →

If browser, web app, API, CRM and marketing platform are involved, I want to know exactly what leaves each system, what the next one expects and what evidence exists at the handoff.

SEP 2026

Design the exit before the message. →

For any triggered journey, ask what business event should make the message irrelevant. The exit condition is part of the business rule, not an afterthought.

Noteworthy.

A small list of material I think is worth revisiting. Books link to an official publisher or author page; the practice items open into my own notes.

BOOK / SYSTEMS ↗

Thinking in Systems — Donella Meadows

A useful reminder that fixing the visible output is not the same as changing the system that produces it.

 BOOK / OPERATIONS ↗

The Goal — Eliyahu Goldratt

Good for thinking about constraints, flow and why optimizing every local team can still make the whole system worse.

 BOOK / EXECUTION ↗

The Checklist Manifesto — Atul Gawande

I like the central idea: expertise does not remove the need for simple controls when complexity exceeds human memory.

 BOOK / MANAGEMENT ↗

High Output Management — Andrew Grove

Still useful for leverage, operating cadence and thinking about management as a system rather than a personality.

 PRACTICE / INTEGRATIONS →

API documentation before implementation

Read identity, limits, error semantics and the data contract early enough that they can still change the architecture.

 PRACTICE / QA →

Synthetic test users

A reusable set of test profiles across identity, consent and lifecycle states makes end-to-end validation dramatically easier.

SEP 2026 · Operating note

RAID is useful only when it changes behaviour.

A risk register is not valuable because it contains risks. It is valuable when those risks change a decision, owner, sequence or control.

A beautifully maintained RAID log can still be useless.

If a dependency has been yellow for six weeks but nobody changed the plan, assigned an owner or escalated a decision, the team is documenting uncertainty rather than managing it.

I think of RAID as a forcing function. Every meaningful item should answer: what changes because we know this?

Risk management starts when the risk changes behaviour.

Examples of useful consequences.

RAID itemBehaviour change
SignalAction
Source data may arrive lateSequence build around mock data and define a hard reconciliation gate
Identity decision unresolvedStop downstream personalization design until source-of-truth choice is made
Capacity is oversubscribedMake the roadmap trade-off explicit instead of silently slipping work
Consent interpretation unclearEscalate decision before audience logic is finalized

I prefer fewer, more actionable items.

A giant list creates equal visual weight for everything. I would rather maintain a smaller set of items with clear impact, owner, due date, mitigation and escalation path.

The point is not to prove the team identified every conceivable risk. It is to make the risks that can materially change the outcome hard to ignore.

The practical rule.

For every material RAID item, ask what decision, sequence, owner, test or contingency changes because the item exists. If the answer is “nothing,” either the item is not material or the team has not acted on it yet.

SEP 2026 · Operating note

A schedule is not a dependency map.

Dates tell you when. Dependencies tell you whether the date is even possible.

The calendar is usually the visible artifact, not the underlying logic.

In a complicated program, a date can look precise while hiding unresolved questions: Which source owns the data? Who has environment access? Has legal approved the consent model? Is the upstream API available? Has the customer decided which audience definition is authoritative?

If those conditions are unresolved, putting a date beside the task does not make the plan more real. It only makes the uncertainty less visible.

The schedule should be the output of dependency thinking, not a substitute for it.

What I want to know before I trust a date.

What must be true before this work can start?
Which system or team owns each prerequisite?
Which dependency has no committed date?
What decision could change the architecture?
What can proceed in parallel?
What becomes rework if we start too early?

A dependency map changes the conversation.

Instead of asking, “Can development finish by Friday?”, I would rather ask, “If identity rules are approved Tuesday and the source field arrives Wednesday, is Friday still realistic?” The second question exposes the chain of assumptions behind the date.

This is also why I prefer to surface dependencies in stakeholder reporting rather than bury them inside a project plan. A decision owner can act on a dependency. They cannot act on a red box whose cause is unclear.

The practical rule.

Before moving a date, trace the path that creates the date. If the constraint is capacity, solve capacity. If it is a decision, get the decision. If it is an upstream system, expose the dependency. The calendar should move only after the real system has been understood.

SEP 2026 · Technical note

SDK vs REST is usually an ownership question.

The transport decision should follow the source-of-truth decision.

“Which API should we use?” is often the second question.

The more useful first question is: where does the event become true?

A screen view, button tap or in-app search originates on the client. A completed purchase, refund or account-status change may become authoritative on the server. Once that ownership is clear, the transport choice becomes much easier.

Send the event from the system that is best positioned to know it is true.

Client behaviour and business truth are different.

PatternTypical source
EventPreferred ownerReason
Viewed productApp / web SDKThe client directly observes the behaviour
Searched destinationApp / web SDKInteraction happens on the client
Purchase completedBackend / RESTThe server owns the transaction result
Subscription status changedBackend / warehouse syncDurable business state should come from the system of record

Reliability changes the answer too.

If an event must survive a closed browser, intermittent mobile connection or client manipulation, server-side delivery may be safer. If the event is inherently behavioural and useful even before identification, the SDK may be the natural source.

The goal is not ideological purity. It is to avoid having two systems independently claim authority over the same fact.

The practical rule.

Before choosing SDK or REST, write one sentence: “This event becomes true when ___, and ___ is the system that knows that first with enough authority.” Then choose the transport that preserves that ownership.

SEP 2026 · Practice note · QA / lifecycle

Synthetic test users make end-to-end QA dramatically easier.

A reusable set of named test profiles across identity, consent and lifecycle states creates a shared language for proving that customer journeys actually behave as intended.

01 Problem02 Test set03 Rules04 Value

Ad hoc test data makes QA harder than it needs to be.

When every release creates new test users on the fly, teams spend time reconstructing states instead of testing behaviour. One person tests an opted-in customer, another uses a profile with incomplete identity, and a third unknowingly reuses a record whose history already changed the result.

A reusable test profile is not fake data. It is a controlled instrument for proving system behaviour.

I prefer a small, named test set.

The exact profiles depend on the program, but the structure usually covers the important branches:

ExampleReusable lifecycle test set
ProfileStateWhat it proves
TEST-01Known + fully consentedHappy path / intended entry and message
TEST-02Known + opted outSuppression / consent enforcement
TEST-03Anonymous → identifiedIdentity transition and profile continuity
TEST-04Eligible at trigger, then convertsExit logic before message
TEST-05Missing required source attributeFailure handling / exclusion
TEST-06Duplicate or replayed eventIdempotency / duplicate protection

The profiles need operating rules.

  • Give each profile a stable purpose and owner.
  • Document the expected state before each scenario.
  • Reset only what must be reset, and record when the state changes.
  • Keep identifiers obvious enough that nobody mistakes them for real customers.
  • Use the same profiles across source systems when end-to-end lineage matters.
  • Pair each profile with an expected outcome so screenshots and logs have context.

The value is shared evidence.

Synthetic users make debugging faster because everyone is talking about the same record. Marketing can point to the expected message, engineering can inspect the event and payload, data teams can trace the source record, and QA can compare actual behaviour with a pre-agreed scenario.

They are especially useful for negative tests. It is easy to prove that a message sent. It is more important to prove that the customer who should not receive it did not.

SEP 2026 · Technical note

The system boundary is where I start debugging.

When browser, website, API, CRM and marketing platform are involved, the handoff is often more useful than the product label.

“Salesforce is broken” is rarely a useful debugging statement.

Complex journeys cross systems. Each system can be individually healthy while the overall path still fails because one side sends something the other side does not expect.

That is why I start with the boundaries: what leaves system A, what system B expects, what evidence confirms the handoff and who owns each side.

A system boundary turns a vague platform problem into a testable interface question.

The questions are simple.

What exactly leaves the upstream system?
What transport carries it?
What does the downstream system expect?
What evidence exists before the handoff?
What evidence exists after the handoff?
What happens on failure?
Who owns each side?
Can we reproduce it with a known test record?

This is useful beyond APIs.

A browser loading an embedded form is a boundary. A file import is a boundary. A warehouse sync is a boundary. So is a human approval that must happen before development can proceed.

The pattern is the same: define the contract, observe both sides and stop using the end symptom as the diagnosis.

The practical rule.

Draw the path as boxes and arrows. Then replace each arrow with a question: what must cross here, how do we know it crossed and what happens if it does not? Debug the arrows before blaming the boxes.
